issues.body:
TX-STATUS-001 (line 184) requires "a signed `trustx:StatusAttestation`" but never constrains WHOSE signature counts, and TX-EVAL-002 (line 335) only tells the verifier to check "signatures" — with no authorization predicate. The only trust anchor the document establishes is issuer-to-key (line 151, `trustx:trustsIssuer`); the worked example attributes the attestation to `did:web:status.example` (line 199), an entity that appears nowhere in the requirements graph and is not a listed issuer. So a holder-self-signed attestation, or one signed by any key at all, formally satisfies "a signed StatusAttestation positively states trustx:status trustx:valid". That makes the whole positive-status/non-revocation design — the document's central fail-closed property — vacuous as specified.

The asymmetry indicates an omission rather than deliberate scoping: TX-SCOPE-001 (line 259) DOES require a certification to identify its "certifying authority, and verifiable attestation binding". Status attestations get no equivalent obligation.
issues.fix_hint: Add a normative status-authority anchor: a `trustx:trustsStatusAuthority` (or equivalent) term on `trustx:TrustRequirements`, and a MUST that a covering `trustx:StatusAttestation` verify under a key bound to an authority admitted by the requirements resource (directly enumerated, or derived from the framework's trusted-list/register in framework mode). State explicitly that the attester's `prov:wasAttributedTo` value alone establishes nothing, mirroring the existing line-151 sentence for issuers. Add a conformance case for 'status attestation signed by an unanchored key → fail closed'.
issues.title: TX-STATUS-001: the status attester is anchored to nothing — any signature satisfies the letter of the rule

issues.body:
TX-RESP-001 (line 281) requires each reifier to carry `prov:wasAttributedTo` and `trustx:coveredBy`, and TX-EVAL-002 tells the verifier to check "positive status coverage". But the document never defines what makes an attestation *cover* a given statement. A `trustx:StatusAttestation` points at a credential via `trustx:credential` (line 195); nothing requires the reified contributing statement to have been carried by that credential, nor requires the credential to be attributed to the same issuer as the reifier's `prov:wasAttributedTo`.

Consequently a holder can attach a perfectly valid, in-window attestation for credential A to a statement actually derived from revoked credential B and satisfy every stated MUST. The verifier has no defined check that would catch it, because the statement→credential edge is absent from the response encoding entirely (the example at lines 292-298 shows no such link).
issues.fix_hint: Make the credential the unit of coverage and encode the edge: require the reifier to carry the credential it was disclosed from (e.g. `trustx:fromCredential <urn:credential:age-1>`), and define 'covering' normatively as: the attestation's `trustx:credential` equals that credential, the attestation is signed by an anchored status authority, its interval covers the reference instant, and the credential is attributed to the same issuer as the reifier's `prov:wasAttributedTo`. Add a conformance case for 'valid attestation for an unrelated credential → fail closed'.
issues.title: TX-RESP-001: `trustx:coveredBy` is not bound to the contributing statement's credential or issuer

issues.body:
TX-EVAL-002 (lines 337-338) defines the verifier's independent check as "$Q$'s graph patterns conjoined with the admissibility patterns generated from $T R$ over the provenance response". That construction is only valid for monotone, duplicate-insensitive queries, yet TX-REQ-001 (line 78 region) admits any SPARQL 1.1 `ASK` or `SELECT`:

1. Bag semantics / multiplicity. Conjoining provenance-admissibility patterns joins each triple pattern against its reifiers. A statement with two reifiers (two issuers independently attesting the same triple, or two covering attestations) yields two solutions where Q over the admissible subgraph yields one. SELECT cardinality and any `COUNT`/aggregate therefore differ between holder and verifier — a spurious disagreement that this fail-closed contract will resolve as rejection of an honest response, or, with `DISTINCT` masking it, as an undetected multiplicity change.
2. Non-monotone Q. For `MINUS`, `FILTER NOT EXISTS`, `OPTIONAL` + `!BOUND`, the result depends on where the admissibility patterns are conjoined (inside vs outside the negated pattern), and the document gives no rule. Worse, filtering out an inadmissible statement can make a `NOT EXISTS` become true, so 'evaluate over the admissible subset' can yield answers the full dataset does not support — the opposite of failing closed.

This also contradicts the Security Considerations claim (lines 370-371) that "this contract asks only monotone existence questions": nothing in the request contract restricts the query class to make that true.
issues.fix_hint: Either (a) restrict TX-REQ-001 normatively to the monotone, duplicate-insensitive fragment (BGP + join + union + filter over bound values; no MINUS/NOT EXISTS/aggregates/OPTIONAL-unbound tests) and say so where the monotonicity claim is made, or (b) keep the full class and replace the 'conjoin the patterns' construction with 'materialise the admissible subgraph, then evaluate Q unchanged over it', which is well-defined for any Q. If (b), state the multiplicity rule explicitly (one contributing statement contributes exactly one triple to the admissible graph regardless of how many reifiers vouch for it). Add conformance cases pinning a duplicate-reifier SELECT/COUNT and one negation query.
issues.title: TX-EVAL-002: the reference query Q' is not answer-equivalent to evaluating Q over the admissible subgraph

issues.body:
§5.1 (lines 133-135) says "a contributing statement is admissible when it satisfies every condition of at least one resource" — admissibility is decided per statement, so one answer may mix statements admitted under different resources. TX-EVAL-001 (line 331) says the holder "MUST evaluate $Q$ only over statements satisfying one complete requirements resource" — a single resource governs the whole evaluation.

These yield different admissible answer sets, and an implementer cannot tell which is normative. It matters precisely because it is the attack surface §5.4 tries to close: 'MUST NOT combine a partially satisfied direct requirement with a partially satisfied framework requirement' (lines 179-180) rules out mixing *within* one statement's justification, but is silent on mixing *across* statements, which is exactly what the §5.1 reading permits and the TX-EVAL-001 reading forbids.
issues.fix_hint: Pick one and state it once. If per-statement is intended, reword TX-EVAL-001 to 'over statements each of which satisfies every condition of at least one complete requirements resource' and extend §5.4 to say whether two statements in one answer may be admitted under different resources. If per-evaluation is intended, reword §5.1 to say alternatives are selected once for the whole evaluation. Add a conformance case for the mixed-resource answer either way.
issues.title: TX-EVAL-001 contradicts §5.1: per-evaluation vs per-statement requirements-resource selection

issues.body:
The design goals advertise "one reusable RDF trust-requirements graph" (line 51 region) and TX-REQ-002 requires only that *at least one* `trustx:TrustRequirements` resource have a `trustx:question` identifying Q — so TR may legitimately carry resources bound to other queries. But neither §5.1 ("at least one resource") nor TX-EVAL-001 ("one complete requirements resource") restricts the eligible set to `{r : r.question = Q}`.

Read literally, a lenient resource authored for a low-stakes query (say, one enumerating a permissive issuer list) admits statements for a high-stakes Q sent with the same reusable graph. Only the prose aside in §5.4 ("placed in one requirements graph and bound to the same query", line 178) hints that question-binding is load-bearing, and prose in an informative sentence is not a constraint on the MUSTs.
issues.fix_hint: Add the scoping condition to the normative text: in §5.1 and TX-EVAL-001, define the eligible resource set as exactly those `trustx:TrustRequirements` whose `trustx:question` identifies Q, and have TX-EVAL-002 require the verifier to recompute that set from TR rather than trust the holder's selection. Add a conformance case: a TR carrying a permissive resource bound to a different question MUST NOT admit statements for Q.
issues.title: Requirements resources are never scoped to the query, though TR is described as reusable

issues.body:
TX-MODE-FRAMEWORK (line 159) requires a "valid `trustx:Certification`", but 'valid' is never defined for a certification. TX-STATUS-001 (line 185) defines "unrevoked" only "for the credential". The vocabulary table does say a `trustx:StatusAttestation` may attest "a credential or certification" (lines 243-246), and TX-SCOPE-001 requires a certification to carry a validity interval — but TX-RESP-001 requires `trustx:coveredBy` only for the contributing statement, not for the certification.

So a certification that has been revoked by its authority while still inside its `[validFrom, validUntil]` window meets every stated obligation, which is exactly the outcome TX-STATUS-002's fail-closed rule is meant to prevent. The conformance list reinforces the gap: it covers "expired or invalid certification" (line 395 region) but no revoked-certification case.
issues.fix_hint: Define certification validity explicitly as: interval covers the reference instant AND a covering positive `trustx:StatusAttestation` for the certification exists (same coverage definition as for credentials) AND it is signed by the framework's authority. Extend TX-RESP-001 to require `trustx:coveredBy` on the included `trustx:Certification`. Add 'revoked-but-in-window certification → fail closed' to the conformance cases.
issues.title: Framework mode: revocation of the certification itself is undefined, so a revoked in-window certification is accepted

issues.body:
TX-REQ-003 makes a MUST-level anti-replay/anti-substitution requirement — bind the nonce, the "canonical query representation", and the "canonical trust-requirements graph" to the response, and reject a response "whose query or requirements graph differs" — without naming any canonicalization. RDF graph comparison needs a defined algorithm (blank nodes in TR make naive comparison unreliable), and 'canonical query representation' needs at least a rule (algebra form? normalised text?).

As written, two conforming implementations can disagree on whether a response is bound to the right request, and the requirement is not interoperably checkable. The estate already has the pieces (RDF Dataset Canonicalization is used by the zkSPARQL draft), so this looks like an unfinished reference rather than a deliberate open item — and unlike the genuinely-open items elsewhere in the draft, it is not flagged as one.
issues.fix_hint: Name the algorithms normatively (e.g. RDFC-1.0 for TR, plus a stated rule for the query — normalised algebra or exact byte-string with an explicit encoding) and cite them in the references, or, if this is intentionally left open, say so explicitly the way the draft flags its other gaps (SPARQL 1.2 matching, missing vocabulary constants).
issues.title: TX-REQ-003: 'canonical query representation' and 'canonical trust-requirements graph' are undefined

issues.body:
site/test/specs.test.mjs (not in this diff) covers the new entry only via the generic registry round-trip (unique slug, source exists, labelled status). The two sibling drafts whose caveats are acceptance-critical — trust-graph-authz and sparql-crdt — each got a dedicated test in that file pinning their exact honesty phrases and design boundaries against regression.

This draft's value is likewise concentrated in phrases that must not drift: the sq-qhy4 external-audit-pending caveat, 'honest-majority semi-honest only', the inclusive-endpoints rule, and TX-STATUS-002's absence-is-not-validity rule. Nothing currently fails if a later edit weakens any of them. Scoped as minor, not major: four of the six existing drafts have no dedicated test, so this is an established-but-not-universal convention, and the coarse honesty gates (which I ran clean) do catch the phrase/number class.
issues.fix_hint: Add a `test("trust-expression: registered, and its caveats and fail-closed boundaries are present")` block to site/test/specs.test.mjs asserting on the source: /sq-qhy4/, /honest-majority semi-honest only/, /Both endpoints are inclusive/, and the absence-is-not-validity sentence — following the existing trust-graph-authz/sparql-crdt pattern so the assertions go red if a later edit weakens them.
issues.title: No test pins this draft's load-bearing honesty caveats and normative boundaries

issues.body: §7.2 (lines 307-310) says the inverse mapping "maps each such graph IRI back to one reifier and its sole triple term", qualified only by 'exactly one triple per graph and no graph-IRI collision'. But the mapping assigns the reifier "a stable IRI $g$", and the normative example's reifier is a blank node (`_:claim`, line 292) which the TriG example silently skolemises to `<urn:reifier:claim>` (line 317). Skolemisation is not invertible: the inverse cannot recover that the reifier was originally a blank node, and reifier identity is no longer stable across responses in the way an IRI implies. The example also leaves `_:status` as a blank node inside the metadata graph with none of its own properties present.
issues.fix_hint: Extend the losslessness proviso to mention blank-node reifiers explicitly (skolemisation is required and is recoverable only if the Skolem IRIs are marked as such, e.g. the well-known /.well-known/genid/ form), and either give `_:status` an IRI in the TriG example or note that the attestation graph is elided.
issues.title: The informative named-graph mapping is not lossless for blank-node reifiers

issues.body: Lines 302-303 and 381-382 cite `sparq_core::nt`. That module is declared `mod nt;` (private) at crates/sparq-core/src/lib.rs:18, so the path does not resolve from outside the crate and will not appear in rustdoc. The draft does say "internally" / "the internal N-Triples parser" both times, so the statement is honest and not an overclaim — this is purely a reader-navigability nit. (I verified the underlying capability claim is accurate: crates/sparq-core/src/nt.rs does parse RDF 1.2 `<<( s p o )>>` triple terms, object-position only, with a nesting-depth cap.)
issues.fix_hint: Either name a public entry point that reaches the parser, or add three words making the non-public status explicit (e.g. 'the crate-private `sparq_core::nt` module'), so a reader does not go looking for a published path.
issues.title: `sparq_core::nt` is a private module, so the cited path is not resolvable by a reader

verdict.summary:
New Unofficial Proposal Draft (site/specs/trust-expression.typ) plus its registry entry. Verified-good: every named estate symbol resolves (verify_manifest — which really does take trusted_key_set/revocation_policy/nonce; ProofManifest; sparq_trust::{framework_vocab,secprop,admissibility::admissible,vocab::desugar_for_predicate,status_list::{VerifyingLiveStatusCheck,SignedStatusList,justify_status_decision}}; zk_compose::revocation; SEC_REQ_EIDAS20/UK_DVS). The trustx: namespace matches TRUSTX_NS, every table term except credential/status/valid has a shipped constant, and the draft discloses exactly those three gaps. Honesty caveats match repo canon (sq-qhy4 pending; MPC honest-majority semi-honest only, per crates/sparq-mpc/README.md); both build-boundary gates pass locally (no-perf-numbers: 0 findings; privacy-claims: OK). Inclusive [validFrom, validUntil] agrees with framework_vocab's documented closed interval, and the 'SPARQL cannot yet match triple terms' / 'nt parses them internally' claims check out (nt.rs parses <<( )>> object-only; no triple-term surface in sparq-parse). The registry entry parses under build-specs.mjs's regexes and is covered by the round-trip test.

Blocking: the normative core has fail-open gaps. Status evidence is anchored to nothing — no authority binding for a StatusAttestation (unlike TX-SCOPE-001, which does require a certifying authority) and no binding from a contributing statement to the credential its coveredBy attestation covers, so a self-signed or unrelated-but-valid attestation satisfies the letter of TX-STATUS-001. Resource selection is both unscoped w.r.t. trustx:question and self-contradictory (§5.1 per-statement vs TX-EVAL-001 per-evaluation). TX-EVAL-002's reference-query construction is not answer-equivalent under bag semantics or for non-monotone Q, while TX-REQ-001 admits any ASK/SELECT. Certification revocation is undefined in framework mode.
